title: Why to avoid B2C SaaS: churn, price sensitivity, and the dual-funnel exception
summary: Rob argues true B2C SaaS is extremely rare. Most famous examples are content businesses, hardware bundles, or companies that pivoted to B2B. Consumers bring low prices, brutal churn and almost no profitable paid channels. The one consumer-facing model he'd bet on is a dual funnel, where cheap consumer tiers build brand and users while business tiers supply stable revenue.

principles.text: Many supposed B2C SaaS examples aren't. They're content businesses, hardware bundles, or B2B companies in disguise.
principles.quote: True B TOC SAS is extremely rare and most examples of B TOC SAS either pivot to B2B or they only survive at a massive scale.

principles.text: Businesses are far less price sensitive than consumers, so sell where the ROI is obvious.
principles.quote: A $30 expense for a business is a rounding error. They spend more than that on toilet paper in a given week.

principles.text: Low price points need thousands of users and leave no room to pay for customer acquisition.
principles.quote: Low price points and high price sensitivity mean you need thousands or tens of thousands of users to make any kind of money. And you can't spend any money to market to them.

principles.text: Churn climbs as you move down-market. Consumer churn of 10-25% a month makes compounding growth nearly impossible.
principles.quote: If you're selling to consumers, you can see 10, 15, 20% churn. More even more than that. I've seen BTOC businesses with 25% churn.

principles.text: Distribution is the hardest part, not building. Don't count on stumbling into virality; it's rare and orchestrated.
principles.quote: The hardest part is getting folks to care. If you build it, they will in fact not come.

principles.text: Low price does not mean faster growth. It brings lower revenue per user, more support load, higher churn and early plateaus.
principles.quote: Low price means lower revenue per user, higher support load, often higher churn, it's usually going to mean slower growth and early plateaus.
